Private AI

Does your AI live in someone else’s house?

Private AI means the model, the data you send it and the logs it keeps all run somewhere you control: your servers, an in-country cloud, or a locked-down private tenant. You need it when the data is sensitive, regulated or legally required to stay in the country. Everything else can make toast in the cloud.

Bring your AI home See the four options

The fridge test

Before anyone pastes anything into an AI tool, ask one question: would I be comfortable if this sat in a stranger’s fridge for a year?

If yes, use whatever tool is fastest. If no, that job belongs on private AI. That’s it. That’s the strategy. The rest is engineering.

Four ways to run AI, from rent it to own it

Where your AI can live, and what each option is good for
Public chatbotEnterprise cloud tenantIn-country private cloudOn-premises
Where it runsVendor’s shared cloud, often overseasVendor’s cloud under a business contractOpen or licensed models in a cloud region inside your countryYour servers, your building
Good forDrafting, research, brainstormingMost office work, with governanceRegulated industries, government, data-residency rulesCrown-jewel and classified data
Who controls the dataMostly the vendorShared, set by contractYou, in your jurisdictionYou, end to end
Watch out forPersonal accounts, retention, jurisdictionData still leaves your environmentEngineering effort, capacity planningHardware, operations, upgrades

Most organisations run a hybrid: the cloud for the toast, the house for the family recipes.

When you need it (and when you don’t)

You probably need private AI if…

  • The law says where data lives. Saudi Arabia’s PDPL became fully enforceable on 14 September 2024, with a dedicated regulation for transfers outside the Kingdom.
  • Your regulator is watching. Australia’s privacy regulator recommends keeping personal and sensitive information out of publicly available generative AI tools, and overseas AI providers bring cross-border disclosure rules into play.
  • Your customers ask where their data goes in procurement questionnaires.
  • The data would hurt if it leaked: patients, citizens, legal files, M&A, source code.
  • You need real Arabic, not Arabic-ish.
  • You run at volume, where owning the engine beats renting it by the token.

You probably don’t if…

  • It’s public information or low-risk drafting.
  • A governed cloud tool with company sign-in already meets your rules.
  • You haven’t picked a use case yet. Start with the readiness assessment.

Private AI is for the crown jewels, not the cutlery.

How to get there without a two-year programme

  1. Map the data. Crown jewels, confidential, internal, public. One page.
  2. Pick the use case that pays. One workflow, a named owner, a number that should move.
  3. Choose the house. In-country cloud or on-premises, sized for that use case.
  4. Choose the model. Open-weight for most work; a frontier cloud model for hard, low-risk reasoning.
  5. Govern from day one. Access, logging, human sign-off and evidence, mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act or NIST AI RMF.
  6. Ship in 8 to 16 weeks, measure, expand.

Questions people ask

What is private AI?
Private AI is AI where the models, the data you send them and the logs they keep run in an environment your organisation controls: your own servers, an in-country cloud region or a dedicated private tenant, instead of a shared public chatbot.
Is private AI the same as sovereign AI?
They overlap. Private AI is about control: who can see and keep your data. Sovereign AI adds jurisdiction: the data, models and compute stay inside a specific country and under its laws. A government ministry usually needs both.
Do we have to give up ChatGPT, Claude or Copilot?
No. Most organisations run a hybrid: governed cloud tools for low-risk work, private models for confidential and regulated work. The point is choosing where each job runs on purpose.
Are open-source models good enough for enterprise work?
For most business tasks (summarising, drafting, extraction, searching your own documents and agents running defined workflows) current open-weight models are good enough once they are connected to your data and tested. Frontier cloud models still lead on the hardest open-ended reasoning.
What does private AI cost?
More to set up than a subscription, often less to run at volume. The cost drivers are compute (owned or reserved), engineering, and governance. A focused first use case can be live in 8 to 16 weeks.
Can private AI work in Arabic?
Yes. Arabic-first agents on BLDR and a 120+ language translation platform for a Saudi government directorate were built this way, with models and hosting chosen for Arabic and in-region data rules.
